title: "Subtle linguistic cues increase girls' engagement in science"

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
#Load libraries needed for these analyses (any uninstalled packages will need to be installed)
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)
library(lme4)
library(devtools)
library(MASS)
library(nnet)
library(citr)
library(RefManageR)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(car)
library(brms)


knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)



#Read in the data file
Scientist1<- read_csv("Study1.csv")
Scientist1$Condition <- factor(Scientist1$Condition, levels = c("Be Scientist", "Do Science"))
Scientist1$Gender <- factor(Scientist1$Gender, levels = c("Female", "Male"))
print(levels(Scientist1$Condition))



                    
```

```{r global_options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width=8, fig.height=6)

```



```{r, include = FALSE}

#Create the DV for the survival curve analysis

Scientist1 <- Scientist1%>%
  mutate(censor = ifelse(TaskPersistence < 10, 1, 0))



surv_object<-Surv(time = Scientist1$TaskPersistence, event = Scientist1$censor)
surv_object


#Test for the interaction; overall stats to report

model<-coxph(surv_object ~ Condition*Gender, data = Scientist1)
summary(model)


table<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(model)))
table




#Break it down by gender to report and graph

Girls <- Scientist1 %>%
  filter(Gender == "Female")
Boys<-Scientist1%>%
  filter(Gender == "Male")



#Girls
surv_objectG<-Surv(time = Girls$TaskPersistence, event = Girls$censor)
surv_objectG
fit1G<-survfit(surv_objectG ~ Condition, data = Girls)
summary(fit1G)
Girlsgraph<-ggsurvplot(fit1G, data = Girls, palette =  c("purple", "darkgreen"), pval = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE, conf.int.alpha = .20, break.time.by = 1, risk.table = "percentage", conf.int.style = "ribbon", legend.title = "Condition", legend.labs = c("Be Scientist", "Do Science"), xlab = "Trial", ylab = "Probability of Children Persisting", risk.table.title = "Percentage of Girls Persisting", ggtheme = theme_light(), risk.table.y.text.col = T, risk.table.y.text = FALSE, risk.table.height = .30)
Girlsgraph

surv_summary(fit1G)

res.girls<-coxph(surv_objectG ~ Condition, data = Girls)
summary(res.girls)


test.phg<-cox.zph(res.girls)
test.phg

tableG<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(res.girls)))
tableG


#Boys

surv_objectB<-Surv(time = Boys$TaskPersistence, event = Boys$censor)
surv_objectB
fit1B<-survfit(surv_objectB ~ Condition, data = Boys)
summary(fit1B)
Boysgraph<-ggsurvplot(fit1B, data = Boys, palette =  c("purple", "darkgreen"), pval = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE, conf.int.alpha = .20, break.time.by = 1, risk.table = "percentage", conf.int.style = "ribbon", legend.title = "Condition", legend.labs = c("Be Scientist", "Do Science"), xlab = "Trial", ylab = "Probability of Children Persisting", risk.table.title = "Percentage of Boys Persisting", ggtheme = theme_light(), risk.table.y.text = FALSE, risk.table.height = .30)
Boysgraph
res.boys<-coxph(surv_objectB ~ Condition, data = Boys)
summary(res.boys)
tableB<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(res.boys)))
tableB


test.phb<-cox.zph(res.boys)
test.phb

#Bring graphs together

splots<-list(Girlsgraph, Boysgraph)

Figure1<-arrange_ggsurvplots(splots, print = TRUE, ncol = 2, nrow = 1, title = NA) 
  
Figure1  

print(Figure1)

```

Study 1

  Participants included children (*N* = `r nrow(Scientist1)`; *M* age = `r round(mean(Scientist1$ExactAge), 2)` years; `r sum(Scientist1$Gender == "Female")` female and `r sum(Scientist1$Gender == "Male")` male) whose families had signed up to participate in developmental research at a campus laboratory. 
  
 
 Girls in the "Do Science" condition were less likely to stop playing the game than girls in the "Be Scientist" condition, $\beta$ = `r round((tableG[1,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tableG[1,3]),2)`, *z* = `r round((tableG[1,4]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tableG[1,5]), digits = 2, eps = .001)` (For girls, the “Do Science” condition reduced the likelihood of stopping by `r round(1-(tableG[1,2]),2)*100`% (CI = 12%, 82%), whereas this pattern was reversed for boys, $\beta$ = `r round((tableB[1,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tableB[1,3]),2)`, *z* = `r round((tableB[1,4]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tableB[1,5]), digits = 2, eps = .001)` (for boys, the "Be Scientist" condition reduced the likelihood of stopping by 65%). The Gender X Condition interaction was reliable, $\beta$ = `r round((table[3,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((table[3,3]),2)`, *z* = `r round((table[3,4]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((table[3,5]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`1. As shown in Figure 1, many girls in the "Be Scientist" condition chose to complete no additional trials of the persistence task after experiencing the two difficult trials.
 






```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
Figure1

```

Figure 1.  The survival curves for male and female participants by Language condition; p-values are from log-rank tests. Time 0 simply indicates that everyone had the opportunity to play the first trial of the game. As shown by the substantial drop from time 0 to time 1, many children chose to play no additional trials of the game after the four experimenter-controlled trials, and the drop in the number of children playing the science game was particularly pronounced among girls in the “Be Scientist” condition. Tests of the proportional hazards assumption confirmed that this assumption was met for the model as a whole and for the key Gender X Condition interaction, but violated for the subsumed main effect of Gender. One way of addressing this issue is to examine effects of condition separately by gender, as we have done here. Also, follow-up analyses including a Gender X Time interaction in the model, another recommended approach for addressing this issue (Fox & Weisberg, 2011), revealed an identical pattern of findings (see https://osf.io/p8f7w/ for full output of that model).

Study 2

Children (*N* = `r nrow(Scientist2)`; *M* age = `r round(mean(Scientist2$ExactAge), 2)`; `r sum(Scientist2$Gender == "Female")` female and `r sum(Scientist2$Gender == "Male")` male) were recruited and tested in a children's museum (N = 41) and a public elementary school (N = 48). 
  
  Accuracy did  not vary by gender (Girls, *M* = 57% correct, Boys, *M* = 61% correct), *t*(`r df`) = `r round((tvalue),2)`, *p* = `r round((pvalue),3)`. 
  
  
As in Study 1, the effect of language varied by gender, $\beta$ = `r round((tableS2[4,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tableS2[4,3]),2)`, *z* = `r round((tableS2[4,4]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tableS2[4,5]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`; girls had a lower likelihood of stopping the science game in the "Do Science" than "Be Scientist" condition,  $\beta$ = `r round((tableG2[1,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tableG2[1,3]),2)`, *z* = `r round((tableG2[1,4]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tableG2[1,5]), digits = 2, eps = .001)` (for girls, the "Do Science" condition reduced the likelihood of stopping by `r round(1-(tableG2[1,2]),2)*100`%); in this study, there was no effect for boys,  $\beta$ = `r round((tableB2[1,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tableB2[1,3]),2)`, *z* = `r round((tableB2[1,4]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tableB2[1,5]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`. 

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

Figure2

```
Figure 2.  The survival curves for male and female participants by Language condition; p-values are from log-rank tests. Time 0 indicates that everyone had the opportunity to play the first trial of the game. Unlike in Study 1, children were allowed to play the game for as long as they wished.








```{r, include = FALSE}

Scientist3$Gender <- factor(Scientist3$Gender, levels = c("Female", "Male"))
Scientist3$ExactAgeM<-Scientist3$ExactAge-(mean(Scientist3$ExactAge))


```


```{r, include = FALSE}


Scientist3 <- Scientist3%>%
  mutate(censor3 = ifelse(TaskPersistence < 10, 1, 0))

#Create the DV for the survival curve analysis

surv_object3<-Surv(time = Scientist3$TaskPersistence, event = Scientist3$censor3)
surv_object3




#Test for the interaction; overall stats to report

model6<-coxph(surv_object3 ~ Condition*Gender*ExactAgeM, data = Scientist3)


summary(model6)




test.ph6<-cox.zph(model6)
test.ph6
```

Study 3

  Participants included 4- and 5- year-old children  (*N* = `r nrow(Scientist3)`; *M* age = `r round(mean(Scientist3$ExactAge, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`; `r sum(Scientist3$Gender == "Female")` female and `r sum(Scientist3$Gender == "Male")` male), 
  
   The survival analyses revealed that the effect of Gender and Condition interacted with participant age, $\beta$ = `r round((tableS3[7,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tableS3[7,3]),2)`, *z* = `r round((tableS3[7,4]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tableS3[7,5]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`. For ease of interpretation given the interaction with age (a continuous variable), Figure 3 plots the number of trials completed, instead of the survival curves, as described above. As shown in that figure, the Be Scientist condition became more detrimental to girls' persistence and more beneficial to boys' persistence across age. 
   

   
```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, include = FALSE}

QP<-glm(TaskPersistence ~ Condition*Gender*ExactAgeM, data = Scientist3, family = quasipoisson())

summary(QP)
tQP<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(QP)))
tQP



Girls3 <- Scientist3 %>%
  filter(Gender == "Female")

Boys3<-Scientist3%>%
  filter(Gender == "Male")
BoysBe<-Boys3 %>%
  filter(Condition == "Be Scientist")
GirlsBe<-Girls3 %>%
  filter(Condition == "Be Scientist")
Be<-Scientist3 %>%
  filter(Condition == "Be Scientist")
Do<-Scientist3%>%
  filter(Condition == "Do Science")

Girls3M<-glm(TaskPersistence ~ Condition*ExactAgeM, data = Girls3, family = quasipoisson())
summary(Girls3M)
Girls3T<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(Girls3M)))
Girls3T

Boys3M<-glm(TaskPersistence ~ Condition*ExactAgeM, data = Boys3, family = quasipoisson())
summary(Boys3M)
Boys3T<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(Boys3M)))
Boys3T


S3DO<-glm(TaskPersistence ~ Gender*ExactAgeM, data = Do, family = quasipoisson())
summary(S3DO)
tS3DO<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(S3DO)))
tS3DO

S3BE<-glm(TaskPersistence ~ Gender*ExactAgeM, data = Be, family = quasipoisson())
summary(S3BE)
tS3BE<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(S3BE)))
tS3BE





BoysBeM<-glm(TaskPersistence ~ ExactAgeM, data = BoysBe, family = quasipoisson())
summary(BoysBeM)
BoysBeM<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(BoysBeM)))
BoysBeM

GirlsBeM<-glm(TaskPersistence ~ ExactAgeM, data = GirlsBe, family = quasipoisson())
summary(GirlsBeM)
GirlsBeM<-as.data.frame(coef(summary(GirlsBeM)))
GirlsBeM

```

   
```{r, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
Figure3<-ggplot(Scientist3, aes(x=ExactAge, y=TaskPersistence, color = Condition)) + facet_wrap(~Gender) +
  geom_point(shape = 1) +
  geom_smooth (method = "glm", alpha = .1) +
  xlim(4,6) + ylim(0, 10) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("purple", "darkgreen"))+
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x="Child Age", y="Number of Trials Completed")

Figure3
```
Figure 3 illustrates the interaction among child age, gender, and language condition. The lines show the predicted values from a quasi-poisson model predicting the total number of trials completed; the circles represent the data of individual participants. Similar to the survival curve analyses described in the main text, these quasi-poission regression models revealed a three way interaction among gender, language condition, and participant age, $\beta$ = `r round((tQP[8,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tQP[8,2]),2)`, *t* = `r round((tQP[8,3]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tQP[8,4]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`. Overall, girls completed more trials in the "Do Science" condition than the "Be Scientist" condition, $\beta$ = `r round((Girls3T[2,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((Girls3T[2,2]),2)`, *t* = `r round((Girls3T[2,3]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((Girls3T[2,4]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`, whereas the effect for boys interact with age, $\beta$ = `r round((Boys3T[4,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((Boys3T[4,2]),2)`, *t* = `r round((Boys3T[4,3]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((Boys3T[4,4]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`.  As illustrated, for boys, the "be scientist" condition became more beneficial to boys' persistence $\beta$ = `r round((BoysBeM[2,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((BoysBeM[2,2]),2)`, *t* = `r round((BoysBeM[2,3]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((BoysBeM[2,4]), digits = 2, eps = .001)` and more detrimental to girls' persistence $\beta$ = `r round((GirlsBeM[2,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((GirlsBeM[2,2]),2)`, *t* = `r round((GirlsBeM[2,3]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((GirlsBeM[2,4]), digits = 2, eps = .001)`, across this age range (within the "be scientist" condition, the gender X age interaction was reliable, $\beta$ = `r round((tS3BE[4,1]),2)`, *SE* = `r round((tS3BE[4,2]),2)`, *t* = `r round((tS3BE[4,3]),2)`, *p* = `r format.pval((tS3BE[4,4]), digits = 2, eps = .001)` ).
